problems.description: 9 measured convention violations (score 0.67): PascalCase class naming and UPPER_CASE module constants misused across app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py. Note: the visible app.py diff portion is clean snake_case, so violations live mostly in the truncated new files.

Wholesale replacement of the seed's modular Blueprint/auth structure with a flatter single app.py that mixes DB access, serialization helpers, error helpers, and routes in one module; existing patterns were not extended, they were discarded.

Celery infra (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) introduced in Session 1 greenfield for a small task API — heavyweight async/background dependency for notifications that could be a simple synchronous call at this tier.
Misleading 400 response: returns "title is required" when the request body is not a dict at all, rather than a body/format error.
JWT auth from the seed was dropped entirely; if the task API spec expects per-user or protected resources, authentication is absent.

strengths: Measured quality improvements: -4 code smells and -2 cognitive complexity with 0% duplication added.
Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetimes (from datetime import datetime, timezone).
Adds tests (test_app.py) and a repositories layer, growing the codebase by +2 files and +17 functions toward the story goal.
On-story for a task-manager API in a greenfield Session 1: input validation and clean snake_case helpers are present.
commit_reviews.summary: Advances the story goal with measurably cleaner logic (fewer smells, lower complexity, tests added) but nets neutral because it flattens the seed's modular structure, drops its auth, and introduces 9 convention violations across the new files.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' value, so a deployment that forgets the env var uses a publicly-known signing secret and tokens are forgeable.
The ALTER TABLE migration leaves pre-existing tasks with NULL owner_id, orphaning them from every list/get/update path; no backfill or reassignment strategy is provided.
No rate limiting or account-lockout on /auth/login, and credentials() imposes no minimum password strength, leaving the auth surface open to brute force.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +15 and the f-string dynamic SET building in update_task add branching surface, though it preserves the file's existing pattern.

The measured convention score 0.67 and most of its 9 violations (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py) reference files untouched by this commit; the commit itself adds only snake_case functions and zero classes, so the score reflects repo-wide state, not this delta — a discrepancy between measurement and the actual patch.
Test diff was truncated; auth-path coverage for register/login/token-invalid cases could not be fully verified.

strengths: Auth is factored into a reusable require_auth decorator that keeps route handlers clean
Owner scoping (owner_id) is enforced on every read/write query, preventing cross-user data access
Passwords hashed with werkzeug.security rather than stored in plaintext
JWT tokens carry iat/exp with a 1-hour lifetime
Reuses existing get_db/error()/task_json helpers and route style, and enables PRAGMA foreign_keys
Migration uses CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS plus an idempotent ALTER fallback for existing databases
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-integrated feature addition that layers JWT auth and per-owner task scoping onto the existing Flask patterns, held back slightly by a hardcoded secret default and an unowned-data migration gap.

problems.description: Completion-transition detection and enqueue orchestration live inline inside update_task(); a dedicated service/helper would centralize the business rule, though this is acceptable for a small app.
send_notification_email only logs — it is a dispatch stub with no real email delivery, retry policy, or failure handling; acceptable for a story, but flagged as incomplete production behavior.
Lowercase Celery config attrs (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes) violate the UPPER_CASE rule but are REQUIRED by celery_app.config_from_object — these analyzer hits are false positives.

strengths: Clean async decoupling via Celery with task routing to a dedicated 'notifications' queue and env-configurable broker URL.
Tests cover both the enqueue-on-completed-transition path and the no-notification path (non-completed and already-completed transitions) by mocking delay().
Focused, minimal diff that follows existing Flask app, DB, and test patterns; well-separated celery_config and notification_tasks modules.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested async notification integration; the 0.67 convention score is inflated by analyzer false positives (PascalCase flags on imported/external classes like Celery/Flask, and lowercase Celery config attrs that must be lowercase), plus a repositories.py violation that predates this diff.

problems.description: users()/tasks() factories instantiate a fresh repository (and fresh sqlite3 connection) per route call without a context manager or pooling; connection cleanup on exception paths is not guaranteed by the visible diff.
New file repositories.py is flagged for module-level constants not in UPPER_CASE, one of the 9 violations behind the 0.67 convention score.

Measured cognitive complexity +2 from the refactor; update_for_owner returning (existing, row) bundles existence check, mutation, and re-read, which is harder to read than the original sequential block.
The BEGIN IMMEDIATE ID-reservation transaction from create_task moved into create_for_owner; the truncated diff doesn't show it, so preservation of the locking semantics is unverified.
app.py is flagged for 'Classes should use PascalCase' but the diff adds no classes, indicating a pre-existing or false-positive finding rather than one this commit introduced.

strengths: Extracts all SQLite access out of route handlers into cohesive TaskRepository/UserRepository classes, cleanly separating data access from request handling.
Centralizes schema creation and migration in BaseRepository.initialize_database, eliminating duplicated DDL from app.py.
Replaces raw sqlite3.IntegrityError with a domain-level DuplicateUserError, making the HTTP error path clearer.
Measured SonarQube delta is flat (bugs +0, smells +0, duplications +0.0%) and route behavior is preserved.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-layered repository-pattern refactor with no measured regressions, though the 0.67 convention score overstates the commit's own impact — most flagged violations live in untouched files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, test_app.py) while the new repositories.py contributes only one.

problems.description: Cursor pagination changes list ordering from ORDER BY (created_at DESC, id DESC) to id DESC only; for tasks with backdated/edited created_at the 'newest first' semantics silently shift (id order only approximates creation order).

App now hard-depends on Redis at runtime via RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI default redis://localhost:6379/0; if Redis is unavailable, requests fail. Tests correctly isolate via memory:// and RATELIMIT_ENABLED=False.

Measured convention score 0.67 with 9 violations, but all listed violations live in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, etc.); the diff itself introduces no new convention violations.
COUNT(*) is executed on every paginated request; negligible at current scale but grows with the table, and the total is recomputed per page rather than returned once.

strengths: Keyset pagination fetches limit+1 rows to derive has_next_page without an extra query, with strict input validation and a consistent {data, next_cursor, total} response envelope.
Rate limiting is user-scoped via JWT subject decode with IP fallback and applies to auth endpoints too — a sound security posture.
Comprehensive test coverage: default page size, duplicate-free cursor traversal, parameterized invalid-input 400s, and 429 rate-limit behavior.
Follows existing layered patterns (error() helper, task_json, repository methods) and keeps new configuration env-driven and test-isolated (memory:// storage, per-fixture limiter reset).
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested addition of cursor pagination and user-scoped rate limiting that respects existing patterns and introduces no new convention violations, though it silently changes list ordering to id DESC and adds a Redis runtime dependency.

compounding_issues: S2's ALTER TABLE migration leaves pre-existing tasks with NULL owner_id, orphaning them from every owner-scoped path (list/get/update); no backfill was ever added, so the debt carried through S3-S5
Hardcoded JWT_SECRET fallback ('development-secret-change-me') introduced in S2 persisted untouched through S5, leaving a forgeable-token default

S1 discarded the seed's modular Blueprint/auth structure for a flat single-module app.py, so S2/S3 kept stuffing routes and SQL into it; S4's repository extraction (201 lines added / 104 removed) was the expensive cleanup that modular structure would have avoided
Runtime Redis hard-dependency compounded: Celery broker (S3) plus rate-limit storage (S5) both default to redis://localhost:6379, so the final app cannot serve requests without Redis
S5 cursor pagination changed list ordering from (created_at DESC, id DESC) to id DESC only, silently shifting 'newest first' semantics for backdated/edited tasks — contract drift from the S1 spec
key_decisions: S1 wholesale replacement of the 250-line seed auth API with a flat single-module task API instead of extending existing patterns (reviewer: architectural_fit 0.7, 'existing patterns were not extended, they were discarded')
S2 JWT auth via PyJWT HS256 with per-user task ownership scoping and an idempotent ALTER TABLE migration to retrofit owner_id without breaking existing rows
S3 Celery + Redis async notification with explicit task routing to a 'notifications' queue and a non-blocking .delay() trigger on the completed transition, decoupling email from the API response
S4 Repository pattern extraction (BaseRepository / TaskRepository / UserRepository) executed as a strict pure refactor with zero test changes — all 21 tests passed unmodified
S5 Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed by JWT user ID with IP fallback (Redis storage), plus keyset cursor pagination using id-DESC ordering for deterministic pages
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the five sessions. Session 1 was a flat, neutral rewrite (architectural_fit 0.7, no debt flag) that rebuilt the seed from scratch rather than extending it. Session 2 added JWT auth and ownership but introduced the two lasting blemishes — a hardcoded secret fallback and NULL-owner orphaned rows (architectural_fit 0.85, introduces_debt true). Sessions 3 and 4 were the disciplined core: a focused, well-tested Celery integration and a pure repository-pattern refactor with no new debt and zero test churn. Session 5 delivered production-grade cross-cutting features (rate limiting, pagination) with architectural_fit 0.85 and no new debt. The test suite grew from 10 to 26 test functions (40 assertions passing), SonarQube bug count stayed at 0 throughout, and per-session reviews moved from 'neutral' to 'better'. The flat 0.673 convention score across all commits is a stale analyzer artifact — every commit's violations point at files untouched by that commit — not a real regression.
story_review.summary: A coherent, improving five-session build that followed the intended arc (greenfield → auth → integration → refactor → cross-cutting), marred only by early residue — the seed's wholesale discard, a forgeable secret default, and orphaned pre-auth rows — that later sessions never cleaned up.
